paper_context.research_question: Can encoder–decoder neural architectures, augmented with attention and/or multi-task learning using grapheme-to-phoneme data, improve historical spelling normalization given limited annotated training data, and does multi-task learning induce attention-like focusing behavior?
contribution_style: experimental benchmark across many small datasets
architectural comparison (base, attention, MTL, decoding strategies)
diagnostic analyses (parameter comparison, saliency, embedding visualization)
main_claims: Character-based encoder–decoder models outperform prior baselines for historical text normalization across 43 Early New High German texts.
Bidirectional encoding, beam search, lexical filtering and attention improve single-task encoder–decoder performance.

Multi-task learning (MTL) using grapheme-to-phoneme (pronunciation) as an auxiliary task improves normalization performance for models without attention and matches or approaches the gains produced by attention.

Combining MTL with explicit attention degrades performance compared to MTL alone; analyses suggest MTL induces attention-like input focusing, making explicit attention largely redundant in this setting.

Diagnostic evidence (weight correlations, saliency matrices, learned embeddings) supports the interpretation that MTL and attention learn similar input-focus strategies, especially for longer input sequences.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: word-level normalization accuracy (primary empirical metric) across many small/heterogeneous datasets
comparison to existing baselines and prior state-of-the-art
ablation of architectural components (attention, bidirectional encoder, beam search, lexical filtering)
effect of multi-task learning vs single-task (with/without attention)
statistical consistency across datasets (averages, std devs; per-text breakdown)
diagnostic analyses validity: weight similarity, saliency correlation, embedding/t-SNE visualizations
robustness to dataset size and token length (noted limitation for short texts and long inputs)
reproducibility: availability of implementation and clear hyperparameter choices

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that character-level encoder–decoder models (with architectural tweaks) outperform prior baselines for historical spelling normalization across many small Early New High German texts, and that multi-task learning (MTL) using grapheme-to-phoneme auxiliary data induces attention-like input-focusing behavior which makes an explicit attention mechanism redundant or harmful when combined. The empirical backbone is per-text experiments on 43 Anselm texts, reporting word-level accuracy averages and per-text tables. The authors support the MTL≈attention interpretation with three diagnostics: (1) final-layer weight-change correlations, (2) output agreement statistics, and (3) first-derivative saliency correlations plus t-SNE visualizations of learned embeddings/encoder outputs. The logical chain links empirical improvements (Tables 1/4) to architectural choices (bidirectional encoder, beam, lexicon filtering, attention) and to MTL effects. Strengths are broad empirical coverage, consistent evaluation protocol, and multiple complementary diagnostics. Weaknesses and breakpoints include potential evaluation bias from lexical filtering, limited hyperparameter tuning (single dev manuscript), domain-mismatch risk for modern CELEX pronunciations as auxiliary data, statistical treatment of per-text variability and significance, and interpretive gaps in causal claims that MTL 'learns attention'. Several assumptions (e.g., saliency validity, representativeness of first 1,000 tokens, MTL sampling schedule) underpin major inferences but are not fully tested. Overall, the paper presents coherent experimental results and plausible interpretive hypotheses, but some inferential steps (causal interpretation, generalization beyond this dataset/setup) require additional controls and sensitivity analyses.
logical_argument_graph: P0: Historical normalization is important but supervised training data is scarce => motivates small-data approaches.
P1: Character-level encoder–decoder models have small vocabularies and avoid explicit alignments => plausible fit for small-data normalization.
E1: Empirical evaluation on 43 Anselm texts shows encoder–decoder variants outperform baselines on average => supports claim that such architectures are effective (C1).
P2: Architectural additions (bidirectional encoder, beam search, lexical filtering, attention) each provide inductive/practical benefits for decoding quality.
E2: Ablation-style table (Base → Beam → Beam+Filter → +Attention) shows cumulative gains for single-task models => supports claim that components help single-task (C2).
P3: Pronunciation (grapheme-to-phoneme) auxiliary data provides a related inductive bias due to phonology-orthography links.
E3: MTL with CELEX as auxiliary yields average performance comparable to single-task+attention, and improves no-attention models => supports claim that MTL aids (C3, C6).

Observed Empirical Interaction: MTL+attention underperforms MTL alone on averages => leads to hypothesis that MTL induces attention-like focusing that makes explicit attention redundant or harmful (C4).

Diagnostics: (D1) final-layer weight-change correlations between attention-vs-base and MTL-vs-base; (D2) output agreement (resolved/introduced errors and Fleiss κ); (D3) saliency correlations and t-SNE visualizations.
Inference: Converging diagnostics indicate MTL and attention produce similar input-focus patterns (especially for longer inputs) => supports interpretive claim that MTL ≈ learned attention (C5).

Caveats: Several operational and conceptual assumptions (e.g., validity of saliency as attention proxy, lexicon filtering effect, CELEX domain match, single-dev tuning) condition the strength of causal inferences and generalizability.

identified_claims.claim_text: Character-based encoder–decoder models outperform prior baselines (Norma tool, averaged perceptron, bi-LSTM tagger) for historical text normalization on the Anselm corpus (43 texts), yielding higher average word-level accuracy.
evidence: Table 1: Average word accuracies across 43 texts show encoder–decoder variants (e.g., BEAM+FILTER+ATTENTION 82.72%) higher than baselines (Norma 77.89%, Averaged perceptron 75.72%, Bi-LSTM tagger 79.91%).
Per-text results in Appendix A (Table 3 and 4) consistently favor encoder–decoder variants.
uncertainty_flags: Reported gains are averages; per-text variability (std. dev ~2.2–3.2) indicates heterogeneous effects.
Lexical filtering used in some configurations may inflates numbers relative to baselines that did not use identical filtering.

identified_claims.claim_text: Bidirectional encoding, beam search, lexical filtering and adding attention improve single-task encoder–decoder performance cumulatively.
evidence: Table 4: progression GREEDY 78.91% → BEAM 79.27% → BEAM+FILTER 80.46% → BEAM+FILTER+ATTENTION 82.72% (averages).
Qualitative examples (Sec. 4.1 sample predictions) showing filtering reduces nonsensical outputs.
uncertainty_flags: Benefit magnitudes vary across texts; filtering makes some test targets unreachable (~2.25%).
No ablation where lexicon/filter kept identical across baselines to quantify potential evaluation bias.

identified_claims.claim_text: Multi-task learning (MTL) using grapheme-to-phoneme auxiliary data improves normalization performance for encoder–decoder models without attention, producing performance on-par with single-task models that include attention.
evidence: Table 1: MTL BEAM+FILTER = 82.76% average comparable to single-task BEAM+FILTER+ATTENTION = 82.72%.
Per-text Table 4 shows many texts where MTL BEAM+FILTER outperforms base single-task variants.
uncertainty_flags: MTL sampling schedule (1 aux per main) and large size/domain of CELEX may influence gains; modern CELEX may mismatch historical phonology.

identified_claims.claim_text: Combining MTL with explicit attention degrades performance compared to MTL alone; analyses suggest MTL induces attention-like input focusing behavior, making explicit attention largely redundant in this setting.
evidence: Table 1: MTL BEAM+FILTER = 82.76% vs MTL BEAM+FILTER+ATTENTION = 82.02% (average decrease).
Textual claim in Sec. 4.1 that attention 'hurts' multi-task architecture performance.
uncertainty_flags: Decrease is modest on averages and could depend on attention hyperparameters or implementation; no exploration of alternative attention variants reported.
Causality (MTL causing attention redundancy) is inferred from correlational diagnostics, not direct intervention.

identified_claims.claim_text: Diagnostic analyses (final-layer weight change correlations, saliency matrices, learned embedding/t-SNE visualizations) support that MTL and attention learn similar input-focus strategies, especially for longer input sequences.
evidence: Sec. 5.1: Pearson r averaged 0.346 (±0.315) between weight differences; example shows ρ=0.959.
Sec. 5.2: Output agreement statistics: attention resolves 47.7 errors, MTL 45.4, common resolved 27.7; Fleiss κ=0.834 for outputs.

Sec. 5.3: Saliency correlations: an example ρ=0.615 between attention and MTL; systematic analysis across 19k word pairs shows mean ρ=0.303 (±0.177) for input length ≥7, base model correlations |ρ|<0.21.
t-SNE projections show character embeddings/encoder outputs cluster differently under MTL, qualitatively consistent with phonology-driven grouping.
uncertainty_flags: Reported correlation magnitudes vary widely across datasets/examples (high std. dev).
Saliency is only a proxy for 'focus' and may not be strictly comparable to attention weights; t-SNE is qualitative and sensitive to sampling/perplexity.
Different diagnostics yield different effect sizes; together suggest similarity but not direct equivalence or causality.

identified_claims.claim_text: Multi-task learning helps mitigate the shortage of annotated normalization training data by leveraging readily available grapheme-to-phoneme data (CELEX) as an auxiliary task.
evidence: Motivation in Introduction and Sec. 2: CELEX contains 365,530 pronunciations.
Empirical improvements of MTL variants over base no-attention models shown in Tables 1 and 4.
uncertainty_flags: Domain mismatch between modern CELEX and historical spelling may limit transfer; not directly measured.
Benefit magnitude may depend on auxiliary/main sampling ratio and preprocessing choices.

evidence: Authors tuned on manuscript B and report using the same hyperparameters (embedding/LSTM size 128, dropout 0.3, batch 50, 50 epochs) across all texts.
Decision motivated by scarcity of per-text dev data.
uncertainty_flags: Tuning on a single manuscript may bias hyperparameters to that text's properties; no sensitivity analysis shown.

strengths.title: Extensive per-text empirical evaluation
strengths.description: Evaluation performed across 43 heterogeneous Early New High German texts with per-text tables and averaged statistics, providing broad evidence for claims.
evidence: Tables 1, 3, 4 present averages and per-text results; Appendix A includes full per-text scores across 43 texts.

strengths.title: Complementary diagnostic analyses
strengths.description: Multiple orthogonal analyses (weight correlations, output agreement, saliency, t-SNE) are used to support the interpretive hypothesis that MTL induces attention-like focusing.
evidence: Sec. 5 includes weight-change correlation (ρ values), output agreement with Fleiss κ, and saliency correlation analyses across many word pairs.

strengths.title: Pragmatic modeling choices for low-resource setting
strengths.description: Use of character-level seq2seq, single-dev tuning, and lexicon filtering reflect realistic constraints and present a usable recipe for practitioners.
evidence: Sec. 3.1–3.6 discuss model design choices; Sec. 3.6 explicitly defends single-manuscript tuning as realistic for scarce-data scenarios.

concerns.title: Evaluation bias from lexical filtering
concerns.description: Lexical filtering during beam search disallows outputs not present in CELEX+train lexicon, making ~2.25% of test targets unreachable and potentially inflating accuracy relative to baselines that did not use the same filter.
evidence: Sec. 3.3 notes the lexical filter uses CELEX+training targets and that 2.25% of test targets become unreachable; Table 4 shows large gains when filter is applied.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report results with and without lexical filtering for all models (including baselines), and/or compute an adjusted accuracy that excludes unreachable targets so comparisons are fair.

concerns.title: Single-manuscript hyperparameter tuning
concerns.description: All hyperparameters are tuned on one manuscript (B) and applied to all 43 texts; this may bias results and hide sensitivity of methods to hyperparameters across diverse texts.
evidence: Sec. 3.6 explicitly states tuning on manuscript B and applying same parameters across manuscripts; no sensitivity analysis provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a sensitivity analysis: retrain a subset of models with hyperparameters tuned on multiple, diverse manuscripts (or via small grid/random search) and report whether average/per-text results change.

concerns.title: Domain mismatch risk for CELEX auxiliary data
concerns.description: CELEX provides modern German pronunciations which may systematically differ from Early New High German phonology/orthography; this mismatch could produce noisy auxiliary signals or limiting inductive bias.
evidence: Sec. 2 states CELEX (modern German) used as auxiliary data; shared analysis notes domain mismatch risk in assumptions A2.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify domain overlap or mismatch (e.g., measure pronunciation/orthographic divergence statistics between CELEX and historical tokens); alternatively, test MTL with a subset of auxiliary data matched by lemma or phonological similarity.

concerns.title: Interpretive leap from correlation to causation (MTL induces attention)
concerns.description: Diagnostics are correlational (weight-change, saliency, output agreement); claiming that MTL 'learns attention' or causes attention-like focusing needs stronger causal evidence or ablations.
evidence: Sec. 5 uses correlations and agreement statistics to support the conclusion; authors themselves phrase as 'hypothesis' but make relatively strong interpretive claims in abstract/conclusion.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Perform targeted interventions: e.g., train MTL but block the auxiliary classifier gradient contribution to attention-relevant parameters, or train with randomized auxiliary labels to test whether the observed focusing depends on informative auxiliary signal. Report attention-weight vs gradient-saliency alignment statistics under these controlled variants.

concerns.title: Reliance on saliency and t-SNE as primary interpretability tools
concerns.description: First-derivative saliency and t-SNE projections are suggestive but can be unstable and sensitive to hyperparameters; conclusions drawn from them should be hedged or complemented with quantitative tests.
evidence: Sec. 5.3 uses gradient saliency correlations; Sec. 4.2 uses t-SNE with single perplexity choices.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report robustness checks: saliency correlation distributions across random seeds, compare to other attribution methods (integrated gradients, occlusion), and show t-SNE stability across perplexities and seeds.

concerns.title: Statistical testing and per-text significance missing
concerns.description: Averages and standard deviations are reported, but statistical significance tests for differences across architectures and per-text effect heterogeneity are not provided.
evidence: Tables show means and std devs; no p-values, confidence intervals, or paired tests described in manuscript.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide paired statistical tests across texts (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank or paired bootstrap) for key comparisons (e.g., MTL vs single-task+attention, MTL+ATT vs MTL), and report per-text effect sizes and significance to demonstrate robustness.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Uses bi-LSTMs with explicit alignment layer; smaller or different domain; not directly comparable experimental scale.

comparable_works.relevance: Alternative family of methods (character-level SMT) for normalization; conceptual predecessor to character-based neural MT approach.

uncertainty_flags: Lexical filtering makes ~2.25% of test targets unreachable — potential evaluation bias.
CELEX (modern pronunciations) may not match historical phonology; domain mismatch not quantified.
Hyperparameters tuned on one manuscript may not generalize; no sensitivity analysis shown.
Saliency and t-SNE-based diagnostics are interpretive proxies with stability/sensitivity concerns.
Correlational diagnostics do not establish causality for the claim MTL induces attention-like mechanisms.
alternative_interpretations: MTL provides general regularization or improved shared representations (not specifically attention-like focusing); the observed weight and saliency correlations could reflect shared representational shifts rather than a spatial/temporal attention mechanism.

The negative interaction between attention and MTL could be due to implementation/hyperparameter conflicts (e.g., bidirectional encoder + specific attention paramization) rather than true redundancy — alternative attention variants might combine positively.

Lexicon filtering might disproportionately help some architectures (e.g., models that produce plausible but out-of-vocabulary outputs), so observed gains or relative ordering might be partly an artifact of decoding constraints.
transparency_notes: Authors state implementation is publicly available (anonymized link) — facilitates reproducibility; confirm link and include exact training seeds and data splits in released code.
Hyperparameters are listed but optimization details (e.g., weight initialization randomness, early stopping behavior) are reported minimally — include seeds and variance across runs.
Per-text results are provided in appendix, enabling paired statistical tests by downstream reviewers.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The use of modern grapheme-to-phoneme lexicon as an auxiliary MTL signal for historical normalization appears not to have close direct precedents in the provided references; while this is an innovative inductive bias, its validity depends on domain alignment and measured transfer, which needs explicit sensitivity checks.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If CELEX pronunciations closely reflect phonological cues driving historical orthographic variation in the Anselm texts, MTL will provide informative inductive bias and improve generalization.
If auxiliary sampling ratio is appropriately balanced; a different ratio (more/fewer auxiliary samples) could increase MTL benefit or avoid negative transfer.

If lexical filtering is either disabled or applied identically across baselines, the relative ranking of models will still favor encoder–decoder and MTL variants (i.e., gains are not entirely due to decoding constraints).

If alternative attention mechanisms (e.g., different scoring functions, multi-head attention, or attention regularization) are tested and still show negative interaction, the claim of redundancy is strengthened.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Character seq2seq architectures and MTL are established methods; applying CELEX pronunciations as an auxiliary task to historical normalization and the focused diagnostic suite is a methodological variant that appears novel in this specific application, but conceptually incremental.
evidence: Related work cites SMT and some neural attempts (Azawi et al. 2013) but no prior use of grapheme-to-phoneme MTL for normalization is listed.
uncertainty_flags: Determination limited by provided references; broader literature search could surface closer analogs.

novelty_lenses.verdict: potentially insightful hypothesis with conditional impact
novelty_lenses.rationale: The suggestion that informative auxiliary tasks can induce attention-like focusing (making explicit attention redundant) is a conceptually interesting claim that, if robust across tasks and datasets, could influence how MTL is used as an implicit alignment mechanism.
evidence: Converging diagnostics (weights, saliency, outputs) show consistent similarity between MTL and attention in this dataset and setup.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper empirically evaluates character-level encoder–decoder (LSTM) models for historical spelling normalization across 43 Early New High German texts, comparing base, beam search, lexical filtering, attentional, and multi-task learning (MTL using CELEX grapheme-to-phoneme data) variants. Primary empirical findings: encoder–decoder models outperform prior baselines on average; bidirectional encoding, beam search, lexical filtering and attention improve single-task performance; MTL with pronunciation data substantially helps non-attentional models and yields performance comparable to single-task attention; combining MTL+explicit attention degrades results. The authors support the MTL≈attention claim using three diagnostic analyses: (1) final-layer weight-change correlations between attention and MTL models, (2) output agreement statistics (resolved/introduced errors and Fleiss κ), and (3) first-derivative saliency correlations (gradient-based importance) and t-SNE visualizations of learned embeddings. Key operational choices: hyperparameters tuned on a single manuscript (B) and used for all texts; training splits use first 1,000 tokens as test, 1,000 for dev (unused), remainder train; CELEX (modern German) as auxiliary pronunciation data; beam size 5 and lexical filter based on CELEX+training targets. The core methodological questions for validity are (a) robustness of average gains given per-text variance and dataset idiosyncrasies, (b) potential bias introduced by lexical filtering, (c) domain mismatch risks from using modern pronunciation lexicon as auxiliary data, (d) sensitivity of the MTL effect to scheduling/ratio and model hyperparameters, and (e) interpretability limits of weight/saliency/t-SNE analyses for causal claims about MTL inducing attention-like focusing.

Node B: Character-level encoder–decoder models reduce vocabulary and avoid explicit alignments => candidate approach.
Node C: Single-task enhancements (bidirectional encoder, beam search, lexical filtering, attention) improve base model performance => supported by average accuracy increases (Table 1/4).
Node D: Multi-task learning with CELEX grapheme-to-phoneme auxiliary task improves non-attentional models => empirical parity with single-task+attention (Table 1/4).
Node E: Combining MTL+explicit attention degrades performance => observed average decrease (Table 1).
Node F: Diagnostic analyses (weight correlations, output agreement, saliency, embeddings) show similarity between MTL and attention models => interpreted as MTL inducing attention-like focusing.
Node G: Therefore, MTL can act as an inductive bias that replaces explicit attention for this task/setting.

Edges: A->B motivates Node B; B->C tested and supported; B+auxiliary CELEX->D supported empirically; D+attention->E observed negative interaction; F provides mechanistic evidence linking D and attention; from C,D,E,F authors infer G (interpretation).

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Strengthen causal claim by (a) controlled interventions (e.g., ablate parts of the MTL network to see whether predicted focusing patterns change), (b) compare explicit attention weights to saliency systematically across many tokens and models, and (c) run counterfactuals where the auxiliary task is randomized to test whether correlations disappear.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper frames historical spelling normalization as a character-level encoder–decoder sequence transduction problem and evaluates architectural and training variants on 43 Early New High German texts (Anselm corpus). Core methodological variants: (i) base encoder–decoder (LSTM) with greedy decoding, (ii) beam search and lexical filtering, (iii) soft attention with bidirectional encoder, and (iv) a multi-task learning (MTL) setup where grapheme-to-phoneme mappings (from CELEX) serve as an auxiliary task. Empirical results: encoder–decoder models outperform prior baselines on average; beam search, lexical filtering and attention add cumulative gains in single-task models; MTL improves no-attention models to a level comparable to single-task with attention; combining explicit attention with MTL degrades performance. The authors hypothesize MTL induces attention-like input focusing, and support this with three diagnostic analyses: (a) final-layer weight-change correlations, (b) output agreement/error-resolving statistics, and (c) first-derivative input saliency correlations plus qualitative t-SNE of learned embeddings. The paper argues this explains why explicit attention is redundant or harmful for the MTL models in this low-resource historical-normalization setting. Limitations acknowledged by authors and visible in analyses: lexical filter makes ~2.25% of test targets unreachable; hyperparameters were tuned on a single development manuscript and applied unchanged across texts; use of CELEX implies potential domain mismatch; some diagnostics (t-SNE, saliency) are qualitative or variable across datasets. Overall, the manuscript presents an empirically grounded incremental advance (application + MTL variant + diagnostic study) with plausible interpretations but several methodological choices require further probing to rule out alternative explanations.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Historical text normalization is important and labeled data are scarce for supervised methods.
P2: Character encoder–decoder models reduce vocabulary size and remove need for explicit character alignment (advantageous in low-resource settings).
P3: Attention and bidirectional encoders can help sequence transduction tasks with variable-length alignments.
P4: Grapheme-to-phoneme mappings are an auxiliary task available at scale; spelling variation often reflects phonological variation.
A1: Therefore, augmenting encoder–decoder normalization with attention and/or MTL using grapheme-to-phoneme data is a plausible way to improve performance under scarce training data.
M1: Implement base, beam, filter, attention, and MTL variants; tune hyperparameters on one manuscript (B); evaluate across 43 texts using first 1000 tokens as test.
E1: Encoder–decoder variants outperform prior baselines on average (Tables 1,3,4).
E2: Beam, filter, and attention improve single-task models cumulatively (Table 1).
E3: MTL without attention raises no-attention models to parity with single-task+attention (Table 1 and 4).
E4: MTL+attention performs worse than MTL alone (Table 1).
H1: MTL induces attention-like input-focusing behavior, making explicit attention redundant or harmful in this setting.
A2: Test H1 with diagnostics: parameter-weight-change correlations, output agreement/error resolution, gradient-based saliency comparisons, embedding t-SNE.

D1: Diagnostics show moderate-to-strong local agreement between attention and MTL in some measures (weight-change correlations, saliency correlations for longer inputs), supporting H1 but with variability across texts and measures.
C1: Conclude MTL is a practical way to improve normalization under data scarcity and that it can induce attention-like focusing; suggest further work on context incorporation and robustness checks.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper frames historical spelling normalization as a character-level encoder–decoder sequence transduction problem and evaluates several architectural and decoding variants across 43 (44 total, one reserved) Early New High German texts. Motivated by severe per-text data scarcity, the authors augment the main task with a grapheme-to-phoneme auxiliary task (CELEX) via a multi-task learning (MTL) architecture that shares encoder/decoder parameters but has separate output classifiers. Experiments compare base greedy decoding, beam search, lexical filtering (CELEX+train targets), soft attention (with bidirectional encoder), and MTL (alternating one auxiliary sample per main sample) combinations. Empirically, encoder–decoder models outperform several baselines on average; beam search, filtering, bidirectional encoding and attention boost single-task performance; MTL improves non-attentional models to a level comparable to single-task attention; combining MTL and explicit attention degrades performance. To explain the interaction, the authors analyze final-layer weight differences, output agreement, and first-derivative saliency maps, and visualize embeddings via t-SNE. They interpret these diagnostics as evidence that MTL with pronunciation auxiliary data induces attention-like input focusing, reducing or replacing the need for explicit attention. Key operational choices: single-manuscript hyperparameter tuning, trimming training words >14 chars, lexical filtering that makes ~2.25% of test targets unreachable, and evaluation on the first 1,000 tokens per text. The paper's chain: data-scarcity motivation → char-based seq2seq + architectural ablations → CELEX MTL auxiliary supervision → empirical gains and negative MTL+attention interaction → diagnostics supporting MTL ≈ attention hypothesis.
logical_argument_graph: Data scarcity in historical normalization motivates compact models and auxiliary supervision.
Character-level encoder–decoder models reduce vocabulary size and eliminate explicit alignments.
Decoding and architecture improvements (beam search, lexical filtering, bidirectional encoder, soft attention) should improve single-task performance.
Grapheme-to-phoneme supervision (CELEX) is a plausible auxiliary task because orthographic variants often reflect phonology.
Multi-task learning (alternate-sampling scheme) transfers phonological inductive bias to normalization and improves performance for non-attentional models.
Empirical results: encoder–decoder variants outperform baselines; MTL without attention ≈ single-task with attention; MTL+attention decreases accuracy.
Diagnostic analyses (weight diffs, output agreement, saliency correlations, t-SNE) show converging patterns consistent with MTL inducing input focusing similar to attention.
Conclusion: MTL can induce attention-like focusing; explicit attention may be redundant or harmful in this low-resource, CELEX-auxiliary setting.

concerns.title: Domain mismatch risk between CELEX and historical orthography
concerns.description: CELEX supplies modern German grapheme-to-phoneme mappings; historical spelling and phonology differ, so the auxiliary signal may misalign with the normalization task or cause negative transfer for some manuscripts.
evidence: Sec. 2 describes CELEX as modern German transcriptions; Sec. 4.1 and 3.5 rely on CELEX for MTL gains but do not quantify domain mismatch.
Authors note semi-parallel texts with dialectal/time variation; no control experiments with matched auxiliary data.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include ablations that (a) downsample/perturb CELEX phonologies to simulate mismatch, (b) use an auxiliary set more historically aligned if possible, or (c) measure transfer per dialect/time-slice to show robustness.

concerns.title: Single attention implementation and hyperparameters
concerns.description: The negative interaction claim (MTL+attention degrades performance) is based on one soft-attention variant, beam size, encoder directionality and tuned hyperparameters. This may be an implementation-dependent effect rather than a general property.
evidence: Sec. 3.4 uses Xu et al. (2015) soft attention with bidirectional encoder; Sec. 4.1 reports MTL+ATT average drop but no sensitivity analysis across attention variants or hyperparameters.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run sensitivity experiments: vary attention formulations (additive/multiplicative), attention layer sizes, regularization, and MTL sample ratios; report whether negative interaction persists.

concerns.description: Lexical filter restricts beam outputs to lexicon words (CELEX+train targets) and makes ~2.25% of test targets unreachable, which can inflate reported accuracy and confounds comparisons if baselines or other variants do not use identical filtering.
evidence: Sec. 3.3 states filtering using CELEX+training targets and notes 2.25% of test targets unreachable; Table 1 shows BEAM+FILTER improves accuracy.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report results with and without lexical filtering for all models and baselines (or apply identical lexicon constraints to baselines) and quantify accuracy difference caused by filtering.

concerns.title: Saliency as proxy for attention is interpretive and noisy
concerns.description: First-derivative saliency approximates input importance but is a different mathematical object than learned attention weights; reported correlations vary strongly and do not demonstrate mechanism-level equivalence.
evidence: Sec. 5.3 references Li et al. (2016) saliency; systematic analysis yields mean correlation ρ = 0.303 (±0.177) for length≥7, indicating large variance; t-SNE/heatmap examples are qualitative.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Directly compare attention weight matrices (from attentive models) to saliency and to MTL model activations across many examples; include statistical tests per input length bin and show distributions, not only means.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter tuning on a single manuscript risks bias
concerns.description: Tuning all hyperparameters on manuscript B and applying them globally may bias model performance to B's characteristics and obscure whether improvements generalize across manuscript styles.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide either small-scale cross-validation across several representative manuscripts for hyperparameter choice or report performance under different hyperparameter settings to show stability.

concerns.title: Evaluation split and representativeness

The diagnostics triangulate the claim, but causal mechanism is not fully proven.

My confidence is lower regarding the generality and causal interpretation that MTL truly 'learns attention' as a general mechanism because of methodological sensitivities (auxiliary data domain, single attention variant, lexical filtering) that the paper has not fully probed.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper evaluates character-level encoder–decoder LSTM architectures for historical spelling normalization on 43 Early New High German texts (Anselm corpus excluding one development manuscript). Architectural variants (greedy vs beam, lexical filtering, bidirectional encoder + soft attention) and a multi-task learning (MTL) setup that uses CELEX grapheme-to-phoneme pairs as an auxiliary task are compared. Main empirical findings: (1) encoder–decoder variants outperform prior baselines on average; (2) beam search, lexical filtering, bidirectional encoding and attention cumulatively improve single-task models; (3) MTL improves non-attentional models to roughly match single-task attention gains; (4) combining MTL with explicit attention harms performance on average; (5) diagnostic analyses (final-layer weight-change correlations, output agreement/error-resolving stats, gradient-based saliency correlations, t-SNE visualizations) are presented to support the interpretation that MTL induces attention-like input focusing, explaining the negative interaction with explicit attention. Evidence is drawn from averaged word-level accuracies (Tables 1, 3, 4), per-text supplementary tables, and several quantitative diagnostics (Pearson/Fleiss correlations, saliency means/std). Key operational choices that materially affect interpretation include: use of CELEX (modern pronunciations) as auxiliary data, single-manuscript hyperparameter tuning (manuscript B), lexical filtering applied during beam decoding (CELEX + train targets) which makes ~2.25% of test targets unreachable, and training/evaluation splits that take the first 1,000 tokens as test per text. The analyses are generally consistent with the claims but several inferential steps are correlational and contingent on the stated operational choices. I flag uncertainties about generality (other attention implementations, MTL schedules, auxiliary data domain mismatch), potential evaluation bias from lexical filtering, and the interpretive leap from correlation (weight/saliency/output agreement) to causal mechanism (MTL learning attention).
logical_argument_graph: Sparse labeled normalization data motivates a character-level seq2seq (encoder–decoder) approach to avoid explicit alignments and reduce vocab size (Introduction -> Sec.3.1).
Implement base encoder–decoder (LSTM), plus decoding variants (beam, lexical filter) and attention (bidirectional encoder + soft attention) (Sec.3.3–3.4).
Introduce MTL architecture sharing encoder/decoder but separate output classifiers; auxiliary task = grapheme→phoneme from CELEX; training alternates 1 aux per main sample (Sec.3.5).
Evaluate on 43 Anselm texts with fixed hyperparameters tuned on manuscript B; metric = word-level accuracy on first 1,000 tokens (Sec.3.6, 4).

Empirical result: encoder–decoder variants beat baselines on average; beam+filter+attention best single-task; MTL (without attention) attains similar gains to attention; attention+MTL reduces performance (Table 1,4).

Hypothesis: MTL induces an attention-like input focusing strategy; test via diagnostics: final-layer weight-change correlations, output agreement/error resolving stats (Fleiss κ), gradient-based saliency correlations, and t-SNE visualizations (Sec.5).

Diagnostics show nontrivial correlations (weight diffs averaged r=0.346 with high variance; example r=0.959; saliency mean ρ ~0.303 for length≥7; Fleiss κ=0.834), supporting similarity between MTL and attention but not proving equivalence or causality.

Conclude MTL can act as inductive bias that learns input focusing akin to attention under the reported setup, which may make explicit attention redundant or harmful in this low-resource setting (Conclusion).

Diagnostics are correlational; they do not establish the mechanism or causality that MTL 'learns' an attention module.

identified_claims.claim_text: Multi-task learning helps mitigate the shortage of annotated normalization training data by leveraging readily available grapheme-to-phoneme data (CELEX) as an auxiliary task.
evidence: CELEX contains 365,530 pronunciations used as auxiliary supervision (Sec.2).
Empirical improvements are observed for MTL variants relative to base models without attention (Tables).
uncertainty_flags: Auxiliary-modern CELEX may be mismatched to historical orthography/phonology; effectiveness may vary by manuscript/dialect.
No ablation testing alternative auxiliary datasets or sampling ratios is presented.

identified_claims.claim_text: Using a single development manuscript (B) for hyperparameter tuning and then applying the same hyperparameters across all 43 evaluated texts is a realistic setup for scarce-data historical normalization.
evidence: Sec.3.6 explicitly states tuning on manuscript B and using same hyperparameters across all texts.
Per-text evaluations indicate the setup produces competitive performance across many manuscripts.
uncertainty_flags: Tuning on one manuscript may bias hyperparameters to that manuscript's properties; robustness to other tuning choices not shown.
No systematic sensitivity analysis or cross-validation over multiple dev texts is presented.

strengths.title: Extensive multi-text empirical evaluation
strengths.description: Evaluates models across 43 distinct Early New High German texts with per-text results and summary statistics, enabling assessment of robustness across heterogeneous small datasets.
evidence: Tables 1,3,4 and Supplementary per-text tables provide accuracies per text and averages (Sec.4 and Supplementary Material).
Use of Anselm corpus (44 texts) with exclusion of development manuscript B.

strengths.title: Careful architectural ablation and practical choices
strengths.description: Systematic comparison of base encoder–decoder, beam search, lexical filtering, bidirectional attention and a concrete MTL implementation clarifies contributions of each component.
evidence: Sec.3 describes base, decoding variants, attention, and MTL setups; Table 4 reports all combinations per text.
Operational details (beam size 5, lexicon composition, max word length, hyperparameters) are stated.

strengths.title: Multi-pronged diagnostic analysis
strengths.description: Uses complementary diagnostics—parameter weight correlations, output agreement statistics, gradient-based saliency correlations, and embedding t-SNE visualizations—to build a converging argument about MTL effects.
evidence: Sec.5 sections present weight-change Pearson correlations, Fleiss κ for outputs, systematic saliency correlations across 19k word pairs, and t-SNE figures (Figs.2–5).

strengths.title: Pragmatic low-resource setup and transparency
strengths.description: Adopts choices reflecting realistic scarcity (single-dev tuning, character-level models, shared implementation in Keras) and promises code availability.
evidence: Sec.3.6 justification for tuning on manuscript B; Sec.3.7 Keras implementation; Abstract/Intro mention anonymized public implementation.

concerns.title: Lexical filtering alters evaluation outcome
concerns.description: The lexical filter used during beam decoding restricts outputs to a lexicon (CELEX + training targets), making ~2.25% of test targets unreachable and potentially inflating measured accuracy compared to baselines that do not apply the same filter.
evidence: Sec.3.3 notes the lexical filter and a footnote reports 2.25% of test targets are unreachable.
Table 4 shows substantial gains when adding FILTER (BEAM -> BEAM+FILTER).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report controlled experiments without lexical filtering for all models and/or apply identical lexicon constraints to baselines; quantify the per-text effect of filtering by showing delta with/without filter and an adjusted accuracy excluding unreachable targets.

concerns.title: Auxiliary data domain mismatch not quantified
concerns.description: CELEX provides modern German grapheme-to-phoneme mappings; the degree to which these pronunciations align with historical phonology/orthography (and thus provide beneficial inductive bias rather than noise) is not quantified or controlled for.
evidence: Sec.2 states CELEX contains 365,530 modern German forms; Sec.3.5 motivates phonology-orthography link but does not present domain-match diagnostics.
Shared analysis flags domain mismatch risk; authors acknowledge it in Discussion/Conclusion.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include ablation comparing alternative auxiliary sources (e.g., smaller historical pronunciation lexica if available) or controlled noise-insertion experiments; at minimum, analyze transfer effectiveness by measuring MTL gains stratified by lexical overlap / phonological similarity between CELEX and each manuscript.

concerns.title: Inference of mechanism (MTL learns attention) rests on correlational diagnostics
concerns.description: The conclusion that MTL induces attention-like focusing is supported by correlations among weight changes, saliency matrices, and output agreement; these are consistent with the hypothesis but do not establish causal equivalence or the mechanism by which MTL substitutes for explicit attention.
evidence: Weight-change average Pearson r=0.346 with large SD; example r=0.959 shown but is a single-case illustration (Sec.5.1, Fig.4).
Saliency correlations averaged ρ=0.303 for inputs ≥7 chars with SD=0.177; variety across examples noted (Sec.5.3).
Authors use Fleiss κ=0.834 for output agreement (Sec.5.2).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add causal or stronger tests: e.g., lesion the auxiliary task after training, ablate shared components, compare attention-weight distributions to gradient saliency systematically, run controlled experiments where the auxiliary task signal is randomized to test whether MTL’s effect is due to specific phonological structure.

concerns.title: Hyperparameters tuned on a single manuscript without sensitivity analysis
concerns.description: All hyperparameters were tuned on manuscript B and then applied to 43 texts; this is pragmatic but may bias results if B is atypical; no sensitivity analysis or cross-dev checks are reported.
evidence: Sec.3.6 explicitly states hyperparameters were tuned on B and fixed for all texts.
Per-text performance variability exists (Tables show Std. Devs and per-text cells).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include sensitivity experiments: repeat tuning on a held-out different manuscript or perform a small grid/random search on several manuscripts to demonstrate robustness; report whether key conclusions (MTL parity with attention, negative MTL+attention interaction) hold under alternate hyperparameters.

concerns.title: Saliency and t-SNE interpretations need robustness checks
concerns.description: Gradient-based saliency and t-SNE visualizations are qualitative and sensitive to choices (perplexity, sampling); systematic stability checks are not reported, making interpretive claims tentative.
evidence: Sec.5.3 uses Li et al. (2016) first-derivative saliency; t-SNE figures use single perplexities (5 and 7) with qualitative claims (Sec.4.2, Fig.2–3).
Shared analysis notes t-SNE sensitivity and saliency being a proxy for focus.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report robustness: saliency correlations under different random seeds / input subsets, compare alternative saliency measures (integrated gradients, occlusion), and show t-SNE stability across perplexities and multiple runs or use quantitative cluster metrics.

concerns.title: Evaluation split choice may affect representativeness
concerns.description: Using the first 1,000 tokens of each text as test (and 1,000 for dev unused) could be non-representative if the early parts differ systematically; this sampling strategy may bias per-text estimates.
evidence: Sec.4 states the split protocol; shared analysis notes representativeness risk.
No analysis of within-text variation or alternative splits is provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run experiments with randomized test/dev sampling across documents or stratified sampling to check that results are stable to test selection; report any significant differences.

comparable_works.relevance: Primary recent baseline (sequence-labeling bi-LSTM) for historical normalization.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Both use neural sequence models; Bollmann & Søgaard use aligned sequence labeling while current paper uses encoder–decoder without explicit alignment and includes MTL with grapheme-to-phoneme auxiliary.
comparable_works.source_trace: Paper's Baselines section and Table 3; referenced in manuscript.

comparable_works.relevance: Strong rule/Levenshtein-based baseline used in comparisons.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Non-neural rule/learned edit-based system; different output space and no learned encoder representations.
comparable_works.source_trace: Baseline comparisons in Sec.4 and Table 3.

comparable_works.citation_label: Character-based SMT approaches (Pettersson et al., Sánchez-Martínez et al.)
comparable_works.relevance: Earlier character-based translation approaches to normalization.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Conceptually similar problem framing (char→char transduction) but using SMT rather than neural seq2seq; neural approach removes alignment step.
comparable_works.source_trace: Related Work Sec.6 references these SMT works.

comparable_works.relevance: Method used for gradient-based saliency comparisons.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Paper uses first-derivative saliency as a proxy for input importance, following Li et al.'s methodology.

uncertainty_flags: Per-text variability is substantial; averages (±Std Dev) may obscure heterogeneity and potential dialectal/systematic effects.
Lexical filtering makes ~2.25% of test targets unreachable; its net effect on measured gains is not fully quantified across baselines and per-text.
Diagnostic correlations (weight diffs, saliency) show large variance; single-case strong correlations may not generalize.
CELEX (modern pronunciations) may mismatch historical phonology; transfer quality may vary by text and is not systematically measured.
Causal claim that MTL 'learns attention' is interpretive—diagnostics are correlational and do not prove mechanism.
alternative_interpretations: Lexical filtering reduces search errors and prevents nonsensical outputs, making a sizable contribution to improved word accuracy that could explain some gains attributed to architectural changes.

MTL improvements may stem from generic representation regularization (shared encoder/decoder weights) rather than a phonology-specific inductive bias; the auxiliary task may act as a denoising/representation smoothing signal rather than matching attention.

The observed negative interaction between explicit attention and MTL could reflect optimization interference (conflicting gradients from auxiliary and attention-induced parameters) under the chosen training schedule and hyperparameters, not that MTL reproduces attention.
High agreement between MTL and attention outputs could arise because both reduce common base-model errors (e.g., frequent orthographic regularizations) even if their internal mechanisms differ.
transparency_notes: Implementation declared public (anonymized link). Exact random seeds, full hyperparameter search logs, and code for saliency/t-SNE generation should be included to aid reproducibility.
Authors report many relevant hyperparameters (embedding/LSTM size, dropout, batch size, epochs) but do not report stability over multiple training runs / seeds.

Evaluation splits and preprocessing are described; however, the lexical filter causes some targets to be unreachable—this should be explicitly reflected in reported metrics (e.g., adjusted accuracy or reachable-target accuracy).

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: While combining MTL with grapheme-to-phoneme auxiliary data and diagnosing its similarity to attention is not a paradigm-shifting novelty (ties to prior MTL/representation learning literature), applying this specific auxiliary signal to historical-normalization and the observation of negative interaction with explicit attention is a novel empirical finding that requires careful controls to validate.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If CELEX pronunciations systematically reflect phonology behind the historical orthographic variants in many manuscripts, MTL will provide informative inductive bias and improve encoder representations, producing the observed gains.

If the attention implementation or training schedule changes (e.g., stronger attention regularization or different auxiliary sampling ratios), the negative interaction might disappear or invert, indicating sensitivity to hyperparameters rather than a general redundancy.
If lexical filtering is disabled, the relative gains from MTL vs explicit attention may change, revealing how much each technique relies on constrained decoding.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Applying encoder–decoder neural seq2seq to historical normalization and augmenting with grapheme-to-phoneme MTL is an incremental but meaningful methodological variant. The diagnostic connection drawn between MTL and attention is a useful empirical contribution, though not yet mechanistically established.
evidence: Authors state they are first to apply encoder–decoder architectures to historical normalization (Intro).
MTL using CELEX as auxiliary data and multi-diagnostic analysis appears novel for this task.
uncertainty_flags: Novelty relies on absence of prior exactly similar MTL+pronunciation work; no retrieval provided to fully confirm absolute novelty.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Large-scale cross-text evaluation across 43 small heterogeneous datasets and per-text tables provide a valuable benchmark for future work in historical normalization under low-resource conditions.
evidence: Comprehensive per-text results in supplementary tables; systematic comparison to multiple baselines.
uncertainty_flags: Robustness of benchmark conclusions depends on addressing lexical-filtering bias and hyperparameter sensitivity.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Diagnostics suggesting MTL produces attention-like focusing are intriguing; however, the evidence is correlational and requires stronger causal tests to be convincing beyond the reported setting.
evidence: Weight/saliency/output agreement diagnostics (Sec.5) show similarity but with high variability and limited causal tests.
uncertainty_flags: Interpretation sensitivity to chosen saliency metric, attention implementation, and training schedule.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am highly confident in the paper's empirical claims as reported under its stated experimental conditions (results tables, diagnostics). However, medium-to-high uncertainty remains about generalization of the MTL≈attention interpretation and sensitivity to design choices (lexical filtering, auxiliary data domain, hyperparameters), hence a wide confidence interval reflecting evidence strength but interpretive uncertainty.

consensus_findings: Character-level encoder–decoder (seq2seq) models yield higher average word-level normalization accuracy than the cited baselines (Norma, averaged perceptron, bi-LSTM tagger) on the evaluated Anselm corpus under the authors' experimental setup (per-text results and averages across 43 texts support this).

For single-task encoder–decoder models, bidirectional encoding, beam search, lexical (lexicon) filtering, and adding soft attention produce cumulative improvements in average accuracy in the reported experiments.

Multi-task learning (MTL) using CELEX grapheme→phoneme data as an auxiliary task improves non-attentional encoder–decoder models; on average MTL(no-attention) attains performance similar to single-task models that include attention in the reported setup.

Combining the reported MTL setup with the implemented explicit soft-attention variant produced a modest average degradation compared to MTL without explicit attention under the authors' hyperparameters and training schedule.

Multiple diagnostic signals (final-layer weight-change correlations, output-level agreement statistics, and gradient-based saliency correlations, plus embedding visualizations) show non-trivial similarity between MTL and attentive single-task models in many cases—supporting the interpretive hypothesis that MTL produces input-focusing effects akin to attention in this experimental context.
disagreements: Causal interpretation strength: reviewers diverge on whether the diagnostics suffice to claim that MTL 'learns attention' (some view diagnostics as suggestive/correlational and request causal interventions; others treat the converging signals as reasonable provisional support).

Generality of the negative interaction between MTL and explicit attention: some reviewers interpret the observed degradation as possibly implementation- or hyperparameter-specific (attn variant, schedule, tuning), while others see the empirical effect as real within the reported setup but requiring sensitivity checks before broader claims.

Contribution novelty framing: reviewers split between seeing the work as an incremental but useful empirical/methodological variant (encoder–decoder + MTL with CELEX on many small texts) and viewing the MTL→attention interpretive claim as potentially more novel but still provisional pending robustness/causal tests.
uncertainty_hotspots: Lexical filtering: The lexicon-based beam filter makes ~2.25% of test targets unreachable. How much of the reported gains (especially the step BEAM→BEAM+FILTER) are attributable to filtering versus model improvements remains unresolved without ablation results computed for all models and baselines under identical filtering conditions.

Auxiliary data domain match (CELEX): CELEX provides modern German grapheme→phoneme mappings. The degree to which these pronunciations align with Early New High German orthographic/phonological patterns (and thus provide informative versus noisy auxiliary supervision) is unquantified, creating risk of variable transfer or negative transfer across manuscripts.

MTL training schedule and hyperparameter sensitivity: The experiments use a single alternating 1:1 auxiliary:main sampling schedule and hyperparameters tuned on a single manuscript (B). The robustness of MTL gains and the MTL+attention interaction to different auxiliary sampling ratios, learning rates, attention variants, and alternate hyperparameter choices is untested.

Interpretability measures' validity and stability: First-derivative gradient saliency and t-SNE are used to argue MTL produces attention-like focusing, but both methods are sensitive/noisy. Correlation metrics reported have substantial variance across datasets/examples; stability across seeds, attribution methods, and parameter choices is not shown.

Per-text heterogeneity and statistical significance: Averages and standard deviations are reported, but formal paired statistical tests across the 43 texts and analyses of where (which manuscripts/dialects) gains occur are missing; thus it is uncertain which effects are robust versus concentrated in subsets.
model_diversity_effects: Role of attention: In single-task models attention (with bidirectional encoder) consistently improves average performance. However, when the encoder/decoder is trained in MTL with CELEX auxiliary supervision, model behavior changes such that an explicit soft-attention module (as implemented) no longer provides the same benefit and can modestly harm average accuracy—suggesting role-specific interactions where auxiliary-driven shared representations alter how attention contributes.

Role of MTL auxiliary signal: The pronunciation auxiliary appears to (a) regularize and reshape encoder/decoder representations, (b) reduce some classes of base-model errors that attention would otherwise resolve, and (c) change saliency/weight-change patterns. These role-specific effects depend on auxiliary data characteristics (CELEX) and the MTL scheduling, implying that the same auxiliary signal can act as beneficial inductive bias in some model configurations but cause optimization conflict in others (e.g., when combined with the tested attention variant).

Decoding constraints' interaction: Lexical filtering changes the effective output space and interacts with model types differently (it benefits beam-decoded models and may amplify apparent gains of methods that already produce in-vocabulary candidates). This is a role-specific evaluation effect: decoding constraints are not architecture-agnostic and can alter relative rankings.

Practical low-resource setup effect: Tuning hyperparameters on a single development manuscript is an operational role choice that interacts with model diversity—some architectures (e.g., attention variants) may be more sensitive to hyperparameters than others; fixing hyperparameters globally can thus bias comparative outcomes.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Use the authors' reported empirical results and diagnostics as a substantive contribution to benchmarking historical normalization under scarce-data conditions, but request targeted robustness and diagnostic extensions before accepting interpretive claims as mechanistically established. Specifically, ask the authors to (1) provide ablations quantifying the numeric impact of lexical filtering across all evaluated models and baselines (results with and without identical filtering), (2) report paired statistical tests across the 43 texts for the key comparisons (e.g., MTL(no-attn) vs single-task+attention, MTL vs MTL+attention), (3) run sensitivity experiments varying the MTL auxiliary:main sampling ratio and at least one alternative attention formulation and report per-text effects, and (4) add causal or controlled diagnostic checks for the MTL→attention hypothesis (e.g., randomized auxiliary labels, lesioning auxiliary gradients, or training variants that disable the auxiliary after some epochs). Keep the editor role central: require these targeted additional experiments/analyses to reduce key epistemic uncertainties (lexical-filtering bias, CELEX domain-match risk, and causal inference) and to justify any strong mechanistic language in abstract/conclusion.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen empirical claims and mechanistic interpretation, provide (minimum set): (1) Lexical-filter ablation: publish results for all model variants and baselines with the lexicon filter disabled, and/or apply identical lexicon constraints to baselines; report adjusted accuracies that exclude unreachable targets. (2) Statistical testing: include paired tests across manuscripts (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank or paired bootstrap) for all primary contrasts and report effect sizes and CIs. (3) MTL sensitivity: vary auxiliary:main sampling ratios (e.g., 0.25:1, 0.5:1, 1:1, 2:1) and, if feasible, experiment with a small set of alternative attention mechanisms (additive/multiplicative, different attention hidden sizes) and report whether the negative MTL+attention interaction persists. (4) Domain-match diagnostics: quantify overlap/divergence between CELEX and each manuscript (surface n-gram overlap, lemma overlap, phoneme distribution distance); if possible, run an auxiliary ablation using perturbed or randomized CELEX labels to test whether the benefit depends on informative phonological structure. (5) Interpretability robustness: replicate saliency analyses with at least one alternate attribution method (e.g., integrated gradients or occlusion), show distributions across seeds/examples and per input-length bins, and compare attentional weight matrices directly to saliency maps where attention is present. (6) Reproducibility artifacts: release code, exact preprocessing scripts, lexicons, random seeds, and scripts to reproduce saliency/t-SNE figures. In reporting, moderate causal language about MTL 'learning attention' unless causal tests are added; instead, characterize findings as converging evidence that MTL produces attention-like input-focus patterns under the reported conditions.
transparency_report: Strengths in transparency: per-text results across all evaluated manuscripts are provided in supplementary material; model architectures, primary hyperparameter values, dataset splits, and the auxiliary CELEX resource are described; authors indicate public code release (anonymized link).

Gaps to rectify: exact lexicon used for filtering (composition and preprocessing), code/config to reproduce lexical-filter ablation, random seeds and ML framework/library versions, full training logs (loss curves, early stopping behavior) and scripts for saliency/t-SNE reproduction are not fully detailed in the manuscript and should be included in the released repository.

Diagnostics reproducibility: saliency and t-SNE visualizations depend on hyperparameters (perplexity, random seed) and implementation details; authors should publish the parameters and seeds used for those figures and provide batch scripts to regenerate them.
epistemic_limits: The reported evidence supports empirical patterns within the authors' experimental design but does not establish general causal mechanisms. Key limits: (1) Correlational diagnostics (weight-change correlations, saliency similarities, output agreement) can indicate similarity of outcomes or representational shifts but do not prove that MTL implements the same algorithmic attention mechanism. (2) Observed interactions (MTL vs attention) may be specific to the chosen attention implementation, MTL schedule, auxiliary dataset (CELEX), lexicon-based decoding constraints, and hyperparameters tuned on a single manuscript; thus external generalization (other attention types, languages, auxiliary resources, or corpora) is uncertain. (3) The lexicon filtering modifies the reachable output space, introducing an evaluation bias that affects interpretability of accuracy gains unless controlled for. (4) Attribution methods used (first-derivative saliency, t-SNE) are approximate and sensitive to methodological choices; they provide suggestive, not definitive, mechanistic evidence. Overall, mechanistic claims should be presented as hypotheses supported by converging correlational evidence within the evaluated setup; establishing causation requires the additional controlled interventions and sensitivity analyses indicated above.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This empirical study evaluates character-level encoder–decoder architectures (with beam search, lexical filtering, bidirectional encoding, and soft attention) for historical spelling normalization on 43 Early New High German texts, and introduces multi-task learning (MTL) using modern grapheme→phoneme pairs (CELEX) as an auxiliary task. Reported results show encoder–decoder variants improve average word-level accuracy over cited baselines; bidirectional encoding, beam search, lexical filtering and attention provide cumulative single-task gains; MTL (with the reported 1:1 alternating schedule) raises non-attentional models to parity with single-task models that include attention; combining MTL with the implemented soft-attention variant yields a modest average degradation. The authors present converging diagnostics (final-layer weight-change correlations, output agreement/Fleiss κ, gradient-based saliency correlations, and t-SNE embedding visualizations) arguing that MTL produces attention-like input-focusing behavior that can make explicit attention redundant under the paper's conditions. The empirical claims are supported by per-text tables and averages; the mechanistic interpretation is supported by multiple correlational diagnostics but remains inferential pending causal/sensitivity checks.
strengths: Large-scale empirical benchmark: per-text evaluations across 43 heterogeneous Early New High German manuscripts with full per-text tables enabling paired comparisons.
Systematic architectural ablation: greedy vs beam, lexical filtering, bidirectional encoder, explicit soft attention, and MTL variants were compared and reported.

Multi-modal diagnostics: authors triangulate the central interpretive claim via weight-change correlations, output-agreement statistics (including Fleiss κ), gradient-based saliency comparisons, and embedding visualizations.

Operationally pragmatic setup: character-level seq2seq and single-dev tuning reflect realistic low-resource practitioner constraints; implementation details and (anonymized) code release are signaled.
limitations: Lexical-filter evaluation bias: the lexical beam filter (CELEX + training targets) renders ≈2.25% of test targets unreachable. The manuscript does not report parallel results with the filter disabled for all models/baselines, leaving uncertainty about how much of the BEAM→BEAM+FILTER gain is due to decoding constraints versus learned model improvements.

Auxiliary-data domain mismatch unquantified: CELEX provides modern German grapheme→phoneme mappings. The paper does not quantify overlap/divergence between CELEX and the historical Anselm texts or probe whether MTL gains depend on domain alignment; thus risk of noisy auxiliary signal or negative transfer is unresolved.

Hyperparameter and scheduling sensitivity underexplored: hyperparameters were tuned on a single development manuscript (B) and the MTL schedule uses a fixed 1:1 auxiliary:main sampling. The robustness of MTL benefits and the reported negative MTL+attention interaction to different sampling ratios, attention formulations, or hyperparameters is not tested.

Causal interpretation relies on correlational diagnostics: weight/saliency/embedding correlations and output agreement are consistent with the hypothesis that MTL induces attention-like focusing, but these are correlational; causal interventions (lesions, randomized auxiliary labels, controlled ablations) are not presented to establish mechanism-level equivalence.
open_questions: Please provide ablation results for all principal model variants reported (base, BEAM, BEAM+FILTER, ATTENTION, MTL, MTL+ATT) with lexical filtering disabled, and/or apply identical lexicon constraints to baseline systems. How much of the reported accuracy gains disappear or persist without the filter?

How sensitive are the MTL gains and the MTL+attention interaction to (a) the auxiliary:main sampling ratio (e.g., 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2), (b) alternative attention implementations (additive vs multiplicative, attention hidden sizes), and (c) hyperparameters tuned on multiple manuscripts instead of manuscript B? Please report a targeted sensitivity grid or representative variants.

Can the authors quantify the domain overlap and divergence between CELEX and each manuscript (e.g., character n-gram / lemma / phoneme distribution overlap)? If possible, provide an experiment using randomized or perturbed CELEX labels (or a downsampled/filtered CELEX subset) to test whether MTL benefits rely on informative phonological structure rather than generic regularization.

For the interpretability claim, can attention weights (from the attentive models) be directly compared to gradient saliency maps (and to activations in the MTL model) across a sizable sample with per-length bin statistics and confidence intervals? Also, could at least one causal intervention be provided (e.g., freeze or remove auxiliary gradients after some epochs) to test whether the MTL-induced focusing is necessary/sufficient for the observed performance?
consensus_snapshot: Encoder–decoder character seq2seq models outperform the cited baselines on average under the authors' experimental setup (per-text results across 43 texts support this).
Beam search, lexical filtering, bidirectional encoding and explicit soft attention cumulatively improve single-task encoder–decoder performance in the reported experiments.
MTL with CELEX auxiliary data improves non-attentional models and, on average, reaches parity with single-task models that include attention for the reported configuration.

Multiple correlational diagnostics show non-trivial similarity between MTL and attentional single-task models, supporting the hypothesis that MTL produces attention-like input-focus patterns in this setup.
disagreement_snapshot: Strength of mechanistic conclusion: reviewers differ on whether correlational diagnostics suffice to claim MTL 'learns attention'—some view converging correlations as reasonable provisional support, others require causal interventions before endorsing that mechanism-level equivalence.

Generality of the negative MTL+attention interaction: some reviewers consider the observed degradation likely specific to the tested attention implementation, MTL schedule, or hyperparameters; others accept it as an empirical phenomenon within the presented setup but recommend sensitivity checks.

Novelty framing: reviewers vary between describing the work as a useful incremental methodological/empirical contribution and highlighting the MTL→attention interpretive claim as potentially novel but provisional pending robustness.
uncertainty_snapshot: Evaluation bias due to lexical filtering (≈2.25% unreachable targets) creates uncertainty in the magnitude of reported gains and relative rankings.
Unknown dependency of MTL benefits on CELEX domain alignment; without overlap statistics or controlled auxiliary-data ablations, transfer validity is uncertain.
High variance in diagnostic correlations across datasets and examples (reported large SDs) reduces confidence in universal mechanistic claims; stability across seeds/attribution methods not shown.
Sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning choice (single-dev manuscript) and fixed MTL scheduling leaves open the possibility that different operational choices change comparative outcomes.
source_trace: CELEX grapheme-to-phoneme resource: Baayen et al., CELEX (dataset referenced in manuscript Sec.2 and used as auxiliary supervision).
Baseline comparisons and sequence-labeling prior: Bollmann & Søgaard (2016) (cited in manuscript Sec.4 as primary bi-LSTM baseline).
Attention implementation reference: Xu et al. (2015) soft attention (Sec.3.4).
Gradient-saliency method: Li et al. (2016) used as precedent for first-derivative saliency analyses (Sec.5.3).

Manuscript-reported diagnostics and empirical tables: Tables 1, 3, 4 and Sec.5 (weight correlations, output agreement, saliency distributions, t-SNE visualizations) as presented in the submitted paper and supplementary per-text tables.
transparency_notes: Per-text results and primary hyperparameters are reported and the authors indicate code release. Remaining transparency gaps to address in the repository/manuscript: (1) exact lexicon composition and preprocessing used for lexical filtering and scripts to reproduce filter/no-filter comparisons; (2) random seeds, ML-framework (Keras/TensorFlow) versions and training logs (loss curves, variance across runs); (3) saliency and t-SNE hyperparameters (perplexities, seeds) and scripts to regenerate figures; (4) scripts/data for reproducing CELEX preprocessing and any mapping between CELEX and training tokens so downstream reviewers can rerun sensitivity/ablation checks.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the paper as a substantial empirical contribution (broad per-text benchmark + diagnostic analyses) but request targeted additional experiments before upgrading mechanistic claims. Required items: (1) provide ablation results with lexical filtering disabled for all main variants and/or apply identical filtering to baselines, (2) include paired statistical tests across manuscripts for the key contrasts (e.g., MTL(no-attn) vs single-task+attention; MTL vs MTL+attention), (3) run a focused sensitivity analysis varying the MTL auxiliary:main sampling ratio and at least one alternative attention formulation to test the negative interaction’s robustness, and (4) add at least one causal diagnostic (e.g., randomized auxiliary labels, freezing auxiliary gradients after training) to probe whether MTL causally induces attention-like focusing. Require these items (or clear justification if infeasible) to reduce the main epistemic uncertainties before presenting the MTL→attention claim strongly in abstract/conclusion.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen claims and reproducibility, please (minimum): (1) report results for all primary model variants with lexical filtering disabled and quantify the exact accuracy delta due to filtering (and list unreachable test targets), (2) perform paired statistical tests across the 43 texts (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank or paired bootstrap) for primary comparisons and report effect sizes and confidence intervals, (3) run sensitivity experiments altering the auxiliary:main sampling ratio (e.g., 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2) and one or two alternative attention variants (additive/multiplicative) and report per-text impacts, (4) quantify CELEX↔manuscript domain overlap (character/lemma/phoneme statistics) and provide at least one auxiliary-data control (randomized/perturbed CELEX labels or downsampled CELEX) to assess whether MTL gains rely on informative phonological structure, (5) bolster interpretability analyses by (a) comparing attention-weight matrices directly to saliency maps across representative samples with per-length-bin statistics and CIs, and (b) replicating saliency with an alternate attribution method (integrated gradients or occlusion), and (6) release code, preprocessing scripts, lexicons, exact seeds, and scripts to reproduce saliency/t-SNE figures. In text, moderate causal language: characterize MTL as producing converging evidence of attention-like input-focus under the reported conditions rather than asserting definitive mechanism equivalence unless causal tests are added.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: This manuscript presents a broad empirical evaluation showing character-level encoder–decoder models (with decoding/architecture refinements) outperform prior baselines across 43 Early New High German texts and introduces MTL using CELEX grapheme→phoneme data, which empirically improves non-attentional models to near parity with attention-equipped single-task models. Diagnostics (weight correlations, output agreement, gradient saliency, t-SNE) provide converging but correlational evidence that MTL induces attention-like input focusing.

Strengths: Large per-text benchmark; systematic ablations and pragmatic low-resource choices; multi-modal diagnostics and public-code promise.

Limitations: (1) Lexical-filtering during beam decoding renders ≈2.25% of test targets unreachable, making reported gains partially dependent on decoding constraints and requiring ablation without the filter; (2) CELEX is modern German—domain overlap with historical texts is not quantified, leaving risk of noisy or non-generalizable auxiliary supervision; (3) hyperparameters tuned on a single manuscript and fixed MTL scheduling (1:1) leave sensitivity questions open; (4) mechanistic claim that MTL 'learns attention' rests on correlational diagnostics without causal interventions.

Open Questions: (1) Provide results (all main variants and baselines) with lexical filtering disabled and quantify the filter’s numeric effect. (2) Explore sensitivity of MTL gains and MTL+attention interaction to auxiliary:main sampling ratios and at least one alternative attention implementation. (3) Quantify CELEX↔manuscript overlap and run an auxiliary-data control (randomized/perturbed CELEX) to probe phonology-specific transfer. (4) Directly compare attention weights to gradient saliency across many examples and, if feasible, include a causal intervention (lesion/freeze auxiliary gradients or randomized labels) to test mechanism.

Transparency: Per-text scores and primary hyperparameters are provided; to ensure reproducibility, release preprocessing/lexicon scripts, exact lexicon used in filtering, random seeds, framework versions, and scripts to regenerate saliency/t-SNE figures. Make filter/no-filter ablation scripts available.

(End of comments.)

The interval encodes reasonable belief that the core empirical phenomena (encoder–decoder improvements and MTL helping non-attentional models) hold under the reported setup, while reserving lower confidence for generalization and mechanistic claims until recommended robustness/causal checks are completed.
